title: ISC2 CISSP
summary: The Certified Information Systems Security Professional (CISSP) is a vendor-neutral, senior-level credential that validates the ability to design, engineer, and govern an organisation's security programme across eight domains of practice rather than a single technology stack. It is aimed at practitioners with several years of hands-on security responsibility who are moving from operating controls to owning risk decisions: security architects, SOC and IR leads, consultants, auditors, and managers who must speak credibly to both engineers and executives. For an employer, a CISSP signals that the holder can reason about trade-offs between confidentiality, integrity, and availability in terms of business impact, select and justify controls, interpret policy and legal obligations, and lead a response when a control fails. The exam is a computerised adaptive test in which question difficulty adjusts to the candidate's running performance; it is scored against a scaled threshold rather than a simple percentage, and questions include advanced innovative items where more than one answer may be technically defensible and the best answer is the one aligned with risk to the business rather than the most technically elegant. Managerial and architectural judgement dominates over command memorisation, so candidates who only read cannot pass. Candidates must also satisfy an experience requirement endorsed by an existing credential holder. Hands-on practice changes outcomes because the domain content only becomes memorable when it is applied: building a risk register, walking an incident through triage to lessons learned, mapping a real architecture against Zero Trust principles, or defending a control choice in writing all convert abstract domain language into the reasoning the exam actually tests. Practitioners who rehearse disaster recovery trade-offs, vendor and supply-chain due diligence, and BCP/DR objective setting under time pressure consistently handle the scenario-heavy items better than those who memorised definitions.
objectives: Security and Risk Management: confidentiality, integrity and availability, security governance principles, compliance and legal obligations, policy and procedure development, business continuity planning, and personnel security.

Asset Security: information and asset classification, ownership and handling requirements, privacy protection, data retention and secure destruction, and establishing handling standards across the asset life cycle.

Security Architecture and Engineering: secure design principles, security models, cryptography and key management, physical security, and site and facility design considerations for resisting and detecting compromise.

Communication and Network Security: secure network architecture and design, network component hardening, secure communication channels, and mitigating attacks against network availability and integrity.

Identity and Access Management: identification and authentication, authorisation mechanisms and access control models, federation and third-party identity services, and the identity life cycle including provisioning and deprovisioning.

Security Assessment and Testing: assessment and testing strategies, vulnerability assessment, penetration testing, security control testing, audit logging, and interpreting test results for decision makers.
Security Operations: investigations and evidence handling, logging and monitoring, incident management, disaster recovery, change and configuration management, and resource protection and continuity.

Software Development Security: integrating security into the development life cycle, secure coding and development environment controls, acquired software and supply-chain risk, and assessing software security effectiveness.
